newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodian forces press into opposition town.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian forces press into opposition town.

text.p: Cambodian government soldiers on Monday pushed into the last town held by loyalists of ousted co-Premier Prince Norodom Ranariddh as the U.N. moved in emergency food, officials said.
In Beijing, Cambodian King Norodom Sihanouk said on Monday he had decided not to abdicate, but also vowed not to return to the political arena in his troubled country.
"After having weighed the pros and cons for many nights, I decide to remain as king for some time longer," Sihanouk said in a statement faxed to reporters.

Ranariddh, Sihanouk's son, was ousted by his coalition partner Hun Sen in early July. His supporters, backed by Khmer Rouge guerrillas, are now making a last stand at the town of O'Smach in northwest Cambodia.
"The government troops have captured the first half, the southern part, of O'Smach," said General Meas Sophea, who heads fighting operations for the government.
"We haven't taken it over yet, but we hope to by tomorrow," he said, adding that dense forest, landmines and the scourge of malaria had made for a difficult advance.

But Khmer Rouge rebels, who have reinforced the royalist positions at O'Smach, offered conflicting reports, claiming they had pushed government forces back to Phong, a town 12 km (seven miles) south of O'Smach.
Major Yen Bunsrun of Ranariddh's army said his forces were fighting with help from more than 1,000 soldiers of the Khmer Rouge, Maoists who ruled Cambodia during the 1975-79 "Killing Fields" years.
Khmer Rouge troops were seen moving on trucks in the area.
O'Smach was quiet earlier on Monday after forces loyal to Second Prime Minister Hun Sen pounded the town with mortar and artillery fire at the weekend.
The United Nations High Commisioner for Refugees (UNHCR) brought in 80 tonnes of rice and 75,000 cans of fish to O'Smach, which is close to the border with Thailand.
About 24,000 people are in O'Smach, many living in poor conditions and fearful of the nearby conflict, officials said.
Ranariddh's forces control a small strip of territory along the Thai border leading to the Khmer Rouge base of Anlong Veng, about 50 km (30 miles) east of O'Smach, Cambodian army officials said.
First Prime Minister Ranariddh's rag-tag forces have been fighting the government in the northwest since the prince was overthrown by Hun Sen in Phnom Penh on July 6.

Hun Sen and Ranariddh formed an uneasy coalition after 1993 elections sponsored by the United Nations. The Khmer Rouge was a party to the 1991 pact that led to the polls but reneged on the deal and waged a low-intensity guerrilla war against Phnom Penh.
Ranariddh had been negotiating a peace deal with the guerrillas for several months and was reported to have reached an agreement just before Hun Sen's power grab.
Hun Sen has justified his actions by accusing Ranariddh of weapons smuggling and illegally bringing Khmer Rouge guerrillas into Phnom Penh.
On Monday, he said in a speech broadcast on local radio that the cooperation between Ranariddh's army and the Khmer Rouge would also be added to the charges against the prince.

In a separate statement, First Prime Minister Ung Huot, who was appointed to replace Ranariddh earlier this month, said the Cambodian government had decided it would guarantee the safety of Ranariddh if he returned to Cambodia, but that the prince still had to face a court upon his return.
Both he and Hun Sen also said that if the prince were found not guilty, they would consider opening talks with him.
Ung Huot invited the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) to send delegates to Phnom Penh to review the evidence against Ranariddh.
ASEAN delayed Cambodia's membership in the wake of the political turmoil in Phnom Penh and has said it wants Ranariddh to be allowed to return to participate in elections next year.
Ranariddh on Monday urged ASEAN to help prevent civil war in Cambodia, warning such a conflict could directly affect the country's neighbours.
